title: Embedded with Burnham: As Britain burns...
gist: A satirical sketch by Henry Morris imagining prime minister Andy Burnham chairing a Cobra meeting during Britain’s sixth heatwave of 2026 to fast-track North Sea drilling licences for the Jackdaw and Rosebank fields, lampooning 'pragmatism' as cover for approving fossil-fuel expansion amid climate catastrophe while Ed Miliband objects.

insights.claim: The satire is set during the UK’s sixth heatwave of 2026, with July described as the driest for 190 years, crop yields down 30 per cent, milk production fallen by 34m litres, and Peak District wildfires smoking out Manchester.
insights.speaker: Henry Morris
insights.so_what: The scene-setting figures dramatise the escalating physical and agricultural toll of UK climate extremes.
insights.quote: July was the driest for 190 years. Crop yields are down 30 per cent. Milk production has fallen by 34m litres.
insights.locator: The UK sweats under the sixth heatwave

insights.claim: The sketch centres on a Cobra meeting convened to fast-track drilling licences for the North Sea energy fields Jackdaw and Rosebank, attended by two fictional Big Oil CEOs alongside cabinet ministers.
insights.speaker: Henry Morris
insights.so_what: Signals that new North Sea licensing remains a live political flashpoint being satirised in real time.

insights.claim: The satire portrays PM Andy Burnham approving the licences on grounds of 'pragmatism'—framing affordable energy bills and working taps as the priority—while dismissing climate objections as unrelatable ideology.
insights.speaker: Henry Morris
insights.so_what: Lampoons how 'pragmatism' rhetoric is used to justify fossil-fuel expansion against scientific advice.
insights.quote: People don’t want ideology. They want to know whether they can afford their energy bills.

insights.claim: The piece has the depicted Ed Miliband argue that new licences won’t lower fuel prices because the output will be sold on the open market, invoking the IEA and IPCC view that oil and gas must stay in the ground.
insights.speaker: Henry Morris
insights.so_what: Restates the core critique that domestic drilling neither cuts bills nor aligns with climate targets.
insights.quote: it’ll all get sold on the open market

insights.claim: The satire depicts oil executives implicitly conditioning their staying in Britain on green-lighting the licences, dramatising industry leverage over energy policy.
insights.speaker: Henry Morris
insights.so_what: Captures the perceived quid-pro-quo between licence approval and corporate investment.
insights.quote: if you green light the licences, perhaps we might be tempted to stick around after all

insights.claim: The sketch’s climax has Burnham repeatedly insisting that a fire alarm, smoke under the door and a failing sprinkler system are all 'unrelated' to climate change, satirising political denial even as the building burns.
insights.speaker: Henry Morris
insights.so_what: A pointed metaphor for governments treating visible climate consequences as reasons for more, not less, fossil energy.
insights.quote: It’s not related to climate change.
insights.locator: Smoke begins to curl underneath the door
